newsitem.title: USA: Chile's Frei says military "respects" democracy.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Frei says military "respects" democracy.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei assured an audience on Tuesday that his country's military, while remaining independent, backs democratic rule.
"We chose to follow a road in 1988 to go back to democracy in a legal way. They (the armed forces) absolutely respect the democratic process ... and we respect the role of the armed forces," he said.

Frei, on the second day of a visit to the United States that will include talks with President Bill Clinton and an address to Congress, was responding after a speech at the University of Chicago to a questioner who asked how Chile could be a true democracy if the military was independent and had its own budget.

The military seized control of Chile in a bloody 1973 coup under Gen. Augusto Pinochet in which President Salvador Allende died and his Socialist-Communist coalition was toppled. Thousands of Chileans were killed, jailed or exiled.

Pinochet lost a 1988 plebiscite and was forced to call elections the next year and hand over power in 1990. But he is still commander-in-chief of the army, which has raised concern that Chile's military are not accountable to civilian rule.

Frei said he wanted to correct a "falsehood going around" that Chile was building up its military. "Chile has one of the lowest investment in armament in the region, about 1.6 or 1.7 percent of the gross national product," he said.

"The only thing we do is maintain our sovereignty and replace old weaponry," he said. "We have arms suitable to protect our territory, our sovereignty. In Chile, we are moving ahead in our rightful and legal goals, and we have respect for the armed forces."
In his speech Frei said Chile was "a nation governed by the rule of law, with independent powers and internal controls ... There is full respect for the law and personal rights are safeguarded."
